A Vector-Symbolic Clojure

Generated with Claude Code, and I am not ashamed. My own blog posts of this kind are part of the training data and have sculpted its style.

Every value is one high-dimensional vector. September 2026, updated October 2026.

This notebook runs a small Clojure in which every value is a single vector of 2048 numbers. That covers lists, maps, sets, integers, closures, and the environment the evaluator runs in. The evaluator never looks inside a vector. It only binds, unbinds, adds and compares vectors, and cleans up noisy ones against a memory.

It is the idea of Tomkins-Flanagan and Kelly’s “Hey Pentti, We Did It!” (2024), which builds Lisp 1.5 this way, carried over to Clojure and then run until it broke. Every result below is computed live when the page renders.

What I learned. Each point is measured below.

  1. Similar is confusable. A cleanup’s margin is 1 minus the similarity to the nearest wrong item. Built as bundles of their parts, the cells of a recursion are 89% alike, and reads fail. Give every structure its own random pointer, shared by equal contents: reads then survive 2.8× more noise. Keep similarity only where you want it, as in vectors.
  2. Never decide with a fixed threshold. A cutoff like “cosine above 0.5” fails at noise σ ≈ 1.7 in every dimension, while the cleanup underneath survives σ ≈ 17. Decide by the best match, or relative to chance (1/√D), and robustness grows with √D.
  3. Convolution commutes, so key–value pairs need direction. Store an entry as k⊗Π(v), with Π a fixed random permutation, as one operation. A cyclic shift does not work, since it commutes with convolution too.
  4. Stored data is robust, computation is fragile. Lists still read back with 60–80% of the dimensions dead; (fact 4) breaks at 2–4%, because every bind passes the damage on until the next cleanup.
  5. A Hopfield network cannot beat a lookup table at exact recall. For a probe that is one stored item plus noise, picking the best match is already optimal. Measured: it ties at best and loses on look-alikes.
  6. Programs can compute on superpositions. A value can be a weighted mix of values, and destructors, arithmetic and if act on all of them at once. This needs a memory that keeps several matches instead of one; it holds about D/100 worlds. It makes no program faster.
  7. An interpreter can live in vector memory. A CEK machine whose 35 rules are vectors, picked by similarity, runs these programs from a host loop of under 50 lines that knows no Lisp.

Why care. Brains, and the neuromorphic chips modelled on them, do not store bits in addresses. They store patterns spread over many noisy units. Vector-symbolic architectures are a mathematical model of how symbols and structure could live in such patterns. A language whose values are all such vectors asks the question concretely: can you program on that kind of substrate, and what goes wrong when you try? It also puts data and code in one format, and it allows a new way of programming, on superpositions of values.

How the interpreter is built, step by step, with all the code: Building a Vector-Symbolic Interpreter.

How the design got here, roughly in the order the traps turned up: History.

Which of the traps exist in the original authors’ own code, holis (2024) and residuelisp (2025), run at pinned commits under the same noise: Reproducing the Traps in the Original Code. In short: holis has trap 3 (its fixed 0.2 caps noise at σ ≈ 5 for every D), and trap 2 when a program names its role vectors; residuelisp has trap 4 (one tag on every integer makes any two integers eq?). Running them also turned up eight further bugs.

Code, tests, experiments and the paper draft: github.com/benjamin-asdf/vector-symbolic-clj.

Hyperdimensional computing in four operations

A symbol is a random vector of D = 2048 numbers. Two random vectors in that many dimensions are almost unrelated: their similarity (the cosine of the angle between them, 1 for equal, 0 for unrelated) is about ±0.02. So there is room for far more symbols than dimensions. Four operations build everything else.

  • Binding a⊗b glues two vectors together, like a name tag onto a value. The result looks like neither, but given one you can get the other back. (Technically: circular convolution.)
  • Unbinding a⊘c peels the tag a off c = a⊗b and gives back b.
  • Bundling a + b throws vectors into one bag. The bag is similar to each thing in it. That is a set.
  • Cleanup snaps a noisy vector to the nearest vector the memory knows, like autocorrect snapping a typo to a real word.

These are holographic reduced representations (Plate, 1995).

Every value is one vector

Start a machine, then read a map into vector space. What comes back is a numpy array, and that array is the entire map.

(vsc/init!)
:ready
(kind/code (str (vsc/eval-form '{:name "Ada" :lang :clojure})))
[0.01107838 0.0151463  0.01316041 ... 0.03630047 0.04730191 0.01519434]

How a list becomes one vector: a list cell says “first is a, rest is b”. Bind a to a fixed role label L and b to a role label R, and bundle the two: L⊗a + R⊗b. To read the first element, unbind L and clean up. Every such cell also gets its own random ID (a pointer), for a reason explained under “What the algebra hides”. The rest of the encoding follows the same pattern. In the table, L, R, V, KEYS, SIZE, B and Z are fixed random vectors, Bⁿ is B bound to itself n times, Π shuffles the dimensions in a fixed random order, and ν rescales to length 1.

value vector
symbol, keyword, string a random atom, stored in the memory M with its kind
(a . b) a pointer p, with M: p ↦ ν(L⊗a + R⊗b)
first, rest unbind L or R from what p points to, then clean up
[x₀ … xₙ₋₁] ν(Σᵢ Πⁱ(V⊗xᵢ)) itself, with no pointer; M records its length next to it
{k v …} p ↦ ν(ν(Σ k⊗Π(v)) + ν(KEYS⊗Σ k) + SIZE⊗n): the entries, the set of keys, and the size n
#{x …} p ↦ ν(ν(Σ x) + SIZE⊗n)
integer n Bⁿ⊗Z, so inc is one more binding with B, and + binds two numbers and unbinds one Z (Bᵐ⊗Bⁿ = Bᵐ⁺ⁿ)
closure p ↦ ν(L⊗form + R⊗env)

Integers are residue numbers (Kymn et al., 2025). At each frequency, B turns by 2π·c/P, with c a random residue of P = 5·7·11·13·17·19 = 1,616,615. Bⁿ is then like six clocks read at once, mixed into every coordinate. Two different integers are unrelated vectors, so a set of integers matches only its members. To read an integer back, the interpreter keeps a memory of every integer it builds or reads (literals, counts, printed values, arithmetic results) and picks the nearest. When arithmetic gets operands the memory does not recognise, or a result that fails its check, the result is read against all of Z_P at once, by one Fourier transform of length P (about 60–85 ms). Integers run from −808,307 to 808,307.

A map is a record: get is one unbind and one cleanup. Map equality ignores key order for free, because addition commutes.

Lists and vectors are encoded differently on purpose. A list is a chain of pointers: robust and unbounded, but two lists that differ in one element are unrelated vectors. A vector puts element i at position Πⁱ and has no pointer, so vectors with the same elements in the same places are similar vectors, and nth is one readout. The price: a vector holds about D/48 elements, and it tolerates less noise than a list, the less the longer it is, because each element gets a smaller share of the vector. The trade-off is the programmer’s choice. Need any number of elements that read back reliably, even under heavy noise? Use a list. Need sequences that are similar when their elements are? Use a vector.

Noise

Add noise as large as the signal to a list, and its first element still comes back, because every read ends in a cleanup.

(examples vsc/run
          '[(first (degrade (quote (a b c)) 100))
            (get (degrade {:a 1 :b 2} 60) :b)])
form result ms 
(first (degrade (quote (a b c)) 100))
 
a

(get (degrade {:a 1, :b 2} 60) :b)

What the algebra hides

Five traps hide in the algebra, and each one shaped the design.

1. Similar lists get confused. In the original paper, a list cell is just the bundle of its parts. Recursion creates many nearly equal cells, such as ((a . 5) . ()) and ((a . 4) . ()), and as bundles they are 89% similar. Reading one of them beats its look-alike by a margin of only 0.05, so a little noise returns the wrong cell, and (fact 5) fails with “unable to resolve symbol: a”. So every cell gets its own random ID, and cells with equal contents share one ID, so checking equality is still one comparison. The right cell then wins by 0.66, and reading survives 2.8× more noise (σ ≈ 11 instead of 4). (Noise σ here means noise of σ times the vector’s own size.)

The lesson is not “never let things be similar”. A cleanup’s margin is 1 minus the similarity to the nearest wrong item, so similarity and confusability are the same number. Lists and the interpreter’s own structures take the margin, and vectors take the similarity.

2. Binding commutes. The original paper binds by circular convolution, and that commutes: a⊗b = b⊗a. Its list cells do not mind, because the labels L and R tell first from rest. A map entry has no such labels. Stored as k⊗v, the entry 1 ↦ 2 is 1⊗2 = 2⊗1, so (get {1 2 2 3} 2) would answer 1.

So an entry is a directed bind, k⊗Π(v), with Π the fixed random shuffle from the table above, and reading it unbinds k and undoes Π. The cheapest permutation, shifting every number one place along, would not do: a shift commutes with circular convolution, so shift(1)⊗2 = shift(2)⊗1. Π goes on the value and not on the key, because keys unbind exactly and a shuffled key no longer does. Pairs without a direction, where a–b is the same as b–a, have their uses too, a symmetric relation for one. They can be a second structure, built on the plain bind.

3. Fixed thresholds throw robustness away. Bigger vectors should tolerate more noise, but a fixed “similar enough” cutoff does not grow with them. Say a value’s kind counts as recognised when its cosine exceeds 0.5. A clean vector’s cosine to its own noisy probe is 1/√(1 + σ²), which crosses 0.5 at σ = √3 for every dimension. So every structure would fail at σ ≈ 1.7, while the cleanup underneath survives σ ≈ 17 at the size of these memories. Deciding by argmax, or relative to the chance level 1/√D, makes robustness grow with √D again, and that is how the interpreter decides. Fixed thresholds are common practice: Nengo’s associative memory defaults to 0.3 in every dimension.

4. A shared field makes strangers similar. If a vector stored its length inside itself, any two vectors of the same length would share that part and look 20% alike, even with no element in common. That is far above chance, and the superposition memory below treats anything above chance as present, so unrelated vectors would creep into results. So the length lives next to the vector in the memory, not inside it. Maps and sets keep their size in their trace, and that is fine: their value is the random pointer p, so two maps of one size are as unrelated as any two pointers.

5. A sum of tuples forgets which values went together. A vector is a sum over its positions, so [1 1] + [2 2] is exactly [1 2] + [2 1]. A superposition of vectors remembers how likely each value is at each position, but not which values occurred together. Tuples whose correlations matter are therefore built as lists.

How robust it is

Here D is the number of dimensions and σ the noise, relative to the signal. A single cleanup matches its textbook model within 0.007 on average, and the noise it tolerates grows as √D: four times the dimensions, twice the noise.

Capacity is linear in D: about D/64 map entries and D/36 set members at 90% reliability. Overloaded structures forget; they do not hallucinate members.

Stored structures survive heavy damage: lists still read back with 60–80% of the dimensions dead, sets with 60–80%, maps with 26–56%. A long computation such as (fact 4) survives 2–4%, because every bind re-loses the dead dimensions until the next cleanup. A short one, (+ 17 25), survives about half.

Hopfield networks do not help

The paper suggests a modern Hopfield network as the cleanup memory. Instead of returning the one best match, it returns a weighted mix of the stored items, and can repeat that step. A parameter β sets how hard it favours the best match: at large β the mix is almost only the winner.

It cannot beat a plain lookup table here, and the reason comes before any experiment. Every probe the interpreter makes is one stored item plus noise, and for such a probe picking the single best match is already the best possible decision. The Hopfield network scores the same stored items the same way, so its first step picks the table’s winner at every β, and repeating the step only sharpens whatever was ahead. It can tie the table or lose to it, and the experiments measure where it loses.

With unrelated stored items, β = 64 is the table, only slower, and smaller β is worse:

Stored look-alikes are where it loses. In groups of 16 items at similarity 7/8, β = 64 still holds for three steps, but ten steps pull the state towards the centre of the group; only β = 256 matches the table there. Inside the interpreter, one soft step at β = 64, which matched the table on unrelated items, passes the blend of look-alikes on as the value. So a well-set β depends on the closest pair of stored items, not only on how many there are. Damage to the stored items costs every memory the same.

noise tolerated (σ₅₀, higher is better) table β = 64, 3 steps β = 64, 10 steps β = 64, 1 soft step
single cleanup, unrelated items 14.1 14.1 14.1 14.1
single cleanup, 16 look-alikes 9.4 9.0 5.6 9.2
reading a vector stored beside 15 look-alikes 3.0 3.0 1.8

So the hope for a Hopfield network is probably not a better cleanup. Exact recall is the one job a lookup table already does as well as anything can. The hope is a different job: a memory of what the computation did, not only of what it stored. Which values a function returned, which code paths a program took. A new situation would then be completed from similar old ones. The pull towards the centre of a group of look-alikes, a loss in the table above, is the same mechanism seen from the other side: it is how such a memory would form a prototype and generalise. That would make the interpreter a neuro-symbolic system, exact where it cleans up and associative where it remembers. The CEK machine below already picks its rules by similarity; a memory of its past runs would be the next step. I have not built it.

The interpreter as vectors

The evaluator above is host code. The next step moves it into vectors. A classic design for interpreters, the CEK machine, keeps three things: the Control, what to evaluate now; the Environment, which variable has which value; and the Kontinuation, a to-do list of what comes after (spelled with a K by tradition, since C is taken). Here all three, plus a mode, are bundled into one vector: s ↦ ν(C⊗control + E⊗env + K⊗continuation + M⊗mode). Its 35 transition rules sit in a memory and are picked by similarity. Rule keys are sums of features, so the most specific matching rule wins by nearest neighbour, and shorter keys act as defaults. The host loop is under 50 lines and knows no Lisp. Tail calls come for free.

One step

The machine runs in steps. Each step goes round the loop below in three phases, and each phase reads some vectors and produces others. The orange lines follow one real step: the moment the machine meets (if (zero? x) :zero (inc x)).

The key is the whole trick. It describes the state by five features: the mode; the kind of C (symbol, number, list, closure, …); the head of C, which matters when C is a list starting with a special form such as if or let; C’s identity, which matters when C is one of the two primitives that re-enter evaluation, apply and eval; and the type of the frame on top of K. Every state’s key has all five; a rule names only those it cares about. Each feature is a random vector bound to its role, and the key is their sum. The rule memory then does what a case statement does in an ordinary interpreter, by similarity.

Here is that step again, decoded live from the vectors. The rule if saves the two branches and the environment in a new frame on K, and makes the test the next thing to evaluate.

decoded from the vectors
the state 
mode EVAL
C    (if (zero? x) :zero (inc x))
K    [halt]
1 · its key 
mode EVAL + kind list + head if + frame halt
2 · the rule chosen 
if
3 · the next state 
mode EVAL
C    (zero? x)
K    [if halt]

The code

The host loop is all the host code there is: fetch, select, run, until the mode is HALT. exec! is the interpreter of the nine instructions. Nothing in it knows about Lisp.

(defn- run-state!
  "Drive the machine from the state in register S until it halts:
  fetch, select a rule by nearest key, run it. Returns the control register."
  [^objects regs]
  (loop [step 0]
    (run-micro! regs (v :fetch))
    (let [[i sim-key pc] (select-rule (reg regs 'KEY))]
      (when (< sim-key theta-rule)
        (throw (ex-info "no rule matches the machine state" {:sim sim-key})))
      (when *trace* (*trace* step i regs))
      (run-micro! regs pc)
      (swap! counters update :steps inc)
      (collect! (reg regs 'S))
      (cond
        (> (sim (reg regs 'M) (named 'HALT)) theta-jump) (reg regs 'C)
        (> (sim (reg regs 'M) (named 'ERROR)) theta-jump)
        (throw (ex-info (str "machine error at " (pr-str (vsc/decode (reg regs 'C)))) {}))
        :else (recur (inc step))))))

(defn- run-micro!
  "Run the microprogram at code pointer `pc` to its end."
  [regs pc]
  (loop [pc pc]
    (when pc
      (let [[ops nxt] (decode pc)]
        (swap! counters update :instrs inc)
        (recur (or (exec! regs ops) nxt))))))

(defn- exec!
  "Execute one decoded instruction on register file `regs`; returns a jump
  target or nil."
  [^objects regs ops]
  (let [a #(nth ops %)
        val #(let [i (a %)] (if (< i n-reg) (aget regs i) (get (v :consts) i)))
        imm #(get (v :consts) (a %))
        put! #(do (aset regs (a 1) %) nil)]
    (case ((v :opcode) (a 0))
      FIELD (put! (field (val 2) (imm 3) ((v :space) (a 4))))
      CLEAN (put! (clean (val 2) ((v :space) (a 3))))
      BIND (put! (bind* (val 2) (val 3)))
      UNBIND (put! (unbind* (val 2) (val 3)))
      REC (put! (store ((v :rec-space) (a 2))
                       (mapcat (fn [k] [(imm k) (val (inc k))])
                               (take-while #(>= (a %) 0) (range 3 n-fields 2)))))
      MOV (put! (val 2))
      JMPEQ (when (> (sim (val 1) (val 2)) theta-jump) (imm 3))
      PRIM (put! (prim (val 2) (val 3)))
      DEF (do (vsc/define! (val 1) (val 2)) nil))))

Everything Lisp-specific is data, assembled into instruction vectors when the machine starts. The instructions:

instruction does
FIELD d x r s d ← cleanup(r ⊘ x): read field r of record x
CLEAN d x s d ← cleanup(x) in memory s, e.g. to classify x by kind
BIND d x y, UNBIND d x y d ← x ⊗ y, d ← x ⊘ y
REC d s r₁ x₁ … d ← a new record ν(Σ rᵢ⊗xᵢ), stored in memory s
MOV d x d ← x
JMPEQ x y l jump to l if x and y are the same vector
PRIM d f x d ← the primitive f (+, first, …) applied to the list x
DEF x y store the global x ↦ y

S, C, E, K, M are the state’s registers; T, A, B, N, X, Y, Z are scratch. (PACK) builds the next state from C, E, K and M, and (JMP l) jumps unconditionally. The fetch phase is itself a microprogram of twelve instructions:

(def fetch-program
  "Unpack the state and compute its shape: the rule key
  ν(FM⊗mode + FK⊗kind(C) + FH⊗kind(C)⊗class(car C) + FI⊗kind(C)⊗class(C) + FF⊗type(top frame))."
  '[:fetch
    [FIELD M S M CONST] [FIELD C S C VAL] [FIELD E S E VAL] [FIELD K S K VAL]
    [FIELD T K T CONST]
    [CLEAN X C KIND]
    [FIELD Y C L VAL] [CLEAN Y Y CLASS] [BIND Y X Y]
    [CLEAN Z C CLASS] [BIND Z X Z]
    [REC KEY NONE FM M FK X FH Y FI Z FF T]])

And the two rules of if. The first fires on the step above. Read with C = (if test then else): X ← the rest of C, (test then else); C ← its first element, the test; A ← the rest, (then else); push a frame onto K that remembers the branches A, the environment E and the old K as its next N; then evaluate C. The second rule fires when the test’s value comes back to that frame: it pops the frame, restores the environment, and evaluates one branch. The frame is gone by then, which is why tail calls come for free.

{:name if,
 :key {:mode EVAL, :kind k-list, :head if},
 :code
 [[FIELD X C R VAL]
  [FIELD C X L VAL]
  [FIELD A X R VAL]
  [REC K W T if-fr A A E E N K]
  [JMP :eval]]}
{:name if-branch,
 :key {:mode RET, :frame if-fr},
 :code
 [[FIELD A K A VAL]
  [FIELD E K E VAL]
  [FIELD K K N VAL]
  [JMPEQ C NIL :if-else]
  [JMPEQ C FALSE :if-else]
  [FIELD C A L VAL]
  [JMP :eval]
  :if-else
  [FIELD A A R VAL]
  [CLEAN X A KIND]
  [JMPEQ X k-empty-list :ret-nil]
  [FIELD C A L VAL]
  [JMP :eval]]}

Why the most specific rule wins. A state’s key always has all five features. A rule’s key names only the features it cares about: a default rule names one, the rule for if names three. When all of a rule’s features match, its similarity to the state’s key is √(k/5) for k features. So when several rules match, the one that names the most features is nearest, and a rule that names fewer acts as a default.

                             [2 "a list is a function call"]
                             [3 "a list headed by if is an if"]]]
                 [k ex (format "%.3f" (Math/sqrt (/ k 5.0)))])})

Superposition programming

A weighted sum of values is also a vector. So a variable can hold several worlds at once, and the program computes on all of them. Destructors act on every world in one memory read, and integer arithmetic lifts exactly, because binding distributes over addition.

(w/init! {:dim 4096})
:ready
(examples worlds
          '[(+ (amb 1 2) 10)
            (first (amb (quote (a b)) (quote (c d))))
            (let [x (amb 1 2)] (+ x x))
            (for-worlds [x (amb 1 2)] (+ x x))])
form result ms 
(+ (amb 1 2) 10)
 
{11 0.5, 12 0.5}
 41 
(first (amb (quote (a b)) (quote (c d))))
 
{a 0.5001, c 0.4999}
 58 
(let [x (amb 1 2)] (+ x x))
 
{2 0.25, 3 0.5, 4 0.25}
 95 
(for-worlds [x (amb 1 2)] (+ x x))
 
{2 0.5, 4 0.5}
 115

Look at the last two rows. A vector carries no labels saying which world a value belongs to, so the two uses of x are independent draws. That is run-time choice. The name comes from nondeterministic programming, where Hussmann (1993) distinguished it from call-time choice, in which a variable picks one value and keeps it. Languages like Curry use call-time choice. Here it is explicit, with for-worlds.

This needed a new kind of memory. A lookup table and a softmax (Hopfield) memory both collapse a sum of worlds to one world. A linear memory keeps the worlds but lets every other stored item through as well. What works is a memory that keeps only the stored items that clearly stand out above chance and solves least squares on them. It holds about D/100 worlds.

if on a superposed test runs both branches and weights them by the test. Each world goes down its own branch, so recursion ends at a different depth in each world:

(w/run '(defn dbl [n] (if (zero? n) 0 (+ 2 (dbl (dec n))))))
dbl
(examples worlds '[(dbl (superpose {2 5 3 3 5 2}))])
form result ms 
(dbl (superpose {2 5, 3 3, 5 2}))
 
{4 0.5, 6 0.3, 10 0.2}
 1229

The weights behave like probabilities, so a textbook Bayesian network works. Rain makes the sprinkler less likely, and either makes the grass wet. What is P(rain | wet)? The exact answer is 0.36255. Probability with such vectors is not new: Furlong and Eliasmith (2024) and the “hyperdimensional transform” (Dewulf et al., 2023) do inference this way. What is new here is that it runs inside an ordinary programming language.

(w/run-string (slurp "examples/worlds/sprinkler.clj"))
#worlds {false 0.6374, true 0.3626}
(examples worlds '[rain-given-wet rain-given-wet-naive])
form result ms 
rain-given-wet
 
{false 0.6374, true 0.3626}
 8 
rain-given-wet-naive
 
{false 0.7998, true 0.2002}
 8

The naive version uses let instead of for-worlds, so run-time choice loses the link between rain and wet grass, and it returns the prior, 0.2. The joint worlds are lists, not vectors. A vector is linear in its elements, so [1 1] + [2 2] is exactly [1 2] + [2 1]: a sum of vectors remembers each position’s distribution, but not which values went together. This query still enumerates the worlds one by one, so it is no faster than ordinary code.

There is no speedup: a superposed step still scans the memory. What superposition buys is a programming model, within a capacity of about D/100 worlds, integers included.

Limits

  • Seconds per small program. Every cleanup scans a memory that only grows.
  • No macros, loop/recur, floats, ordering comparisons or string operations.
  • Records hold about D/64 entries, vectors about D/48; superpositions about D/100 worlds.

What is new here

To my knowledge, these are new:

  • Clojure’s data types as single vectors. Earlier vector-symbolic Lisps encode the cons cells of Lisp 1.5, and integers. Here maps (with directed entries k⊗Π(v)), sets, positional vectors, closures and environments are each one vector too.
  • A catalogue of what breaks. Five traps that the algebra hides, each measured and fixed. One rule covers several of them: decide by the best match or relative to chance, never by a fixed cutoff, and robustness grows with √D.
  • Measurements for a whole language: noise, capacity and damage, with the split between robust stored data and fragile computation.
  • Why a Hopfield cleanup cannot help with exact recall: an argument that holds before any experiment, and the experiments.
  • An evaluator in vector memory. Rules held in vector memory are not new: production systems in HRR (Stewart & Eliasmith, 2008) and a Turing machine with its transition table in an item memory (Kleyko et al., 2022) do it. New is a complete language evaluator run this way: a CEK machine whose 35 rules are picked by nearest key, where sums of features make the most specific rule win, with tail calls.
  • Superposition programming as a language feature. Weighted superpositions are ordinary values. Destructors, lookup, arithmetic and function bodies act on all worlds at once, if splits them, and run-time versus call-time choice is explicit. The semantics has precedents (Lineal; probabilistic functional programming), and so does probability in vectors (Furlong & Eliasmith; Hersche et al.). I know of no language that puts them together on a vector substrate, with a memory that keeps the worlds.

Names “computing in superposition”, and runs a Turing machine whose transition table is an item memory: the closest precedent for rules in vector memory.
